OMK2 · Psychiatry · Introduction to Therapy

Introduction to Therapy

History, theory, and the major psychotherapeutic modalities — from Freud's couch to DBT skills groups.

Lee Wolfrum, DO MHBH at Spring Harbor Medical UNECOM · Psychiatry Discipline Director
Yield check: Therapy itself is not the highest-yield topic for the psych systems exam or boards — but the underlying concepts (conditioning, defense mechanisms, DBT↔BPD, CBT triangle) are recurring test favorites, and the material is clinically essential. Facts flagged ⭐ HY throughout are the ones most likely to show up on an exam.
Section 01

🎯 Objectives & Why This Matters

  • Gain a basic understanding of the history of psychotherapy.
  • Understand the theoretical basis for the major therapies.
  • Compare the different approaches to therapy and the patient populations each is best suited for.

Therapy by the numbers

~10M
people in the US get therapy every year
40%
of people with a therapy-responsive DSM diagnosis who actually receive it — leaving roughly 20M+ untreated
$9.6B vs $13B
spent annually on therapy vs. medications — spending still tilts toward pharmacotherapy
💡
Myth-busting: Popular opinion assumes therapy is mostly for the "worried well" — people with mild complaints. Recent estimates put true worried-well utilization at only 0.5–1% of people receiving treatment. Most people in therapy have a real, functionally impairing diagnosis.

Why people don't get therapy

The barriers cited most often, roughly in order: cost (paired with poor insurance coverage), doubt that talking to someone will actually help, a sense that the problem is "not serious enough" — which often really reflects a person valuing medication over talk therapy — and stigma. Stigma has been softening in recent years as telehealth, app-based protocolized therapy, and even AI-delivered therapy make treatment more private and accessible.

⚖️
Med vs. therapy risk-benefit: For mild-to-moderate depression, anxiety, and especially the personality disorders, therapy is often as effective as medication — without the side-effect burden. Risk-benefit sometimes clearly favors therapy over a prescription, which is worth remembering when a patient asks "can't I just take a pill?"

What actually is "psychotherapy"?

Definitions shift depending on a theory's origins, but most converge on the same core idea: an interpersonal, principle-based treatment delivered by a trained therapist to a patient with a disorder, problem, or complaint, individualized to that patient — using talk, rather than a physical or pharmacologic intervention, to work through emotional distress.

The therapy landscape — where it fits with medications

Dr. Wolfrum builds on the treatment map Dr. Smith uses for mood disorders: biologic treatments (antidepressants, mood stabilizers/lithium, antipsychotics, ECT, psychosurgery/neuromodulation) occupy the "wings" of the map, while psychotherapy is a large, mostly separate branch — humanistic, psychodynamic, cognitive, and behavioral — each with its own techniques. (A reasonable addition to this map: a "lifestyle/physiologic" arrow for sleep, diet, and overall medical optimization, which also affects mood.)

There are ~500 recognized therapy types — this lecture covers the major clouds, not all 500. In practice, most real-world therapy is integrative (mixing modalities): about 33% integrative, 29% psychodynamic, 19% CBT, 6% humanistic by usage.
Section 02

🗂️ Framing Case

Dr. Wolfrum introduces this case early and returns to it conceptually near the end — a useful anchor for the whole lecture.

A 54-year-old financial broker, recently fired

Presentation: A 54-year-old financial broker, recently fired from his job, presents for therapy. History includes stimulant use to perform at work, recent relationship difficulties, and pathologic alcohol use. He arrives in a worn, stained, wrinkled suit; his eyes are bloodshot, speech slow and slurred, eye contact poor. He tells you, "I really need your help, doc."

Working through it with this lecture's toolkit:

  • Multiple overlapping problems — stimulant use, alcohol use, an acute stressor (job loss), and relational strain. This is exactly the kind of presentation where a single "textbook" modality rarely applies cleanly — most real treatment ends up integrative.
  • Motivational interviewing fits naturally for the substance use pieces: exploring the gap between his values (wanting to function, keep his relationship, get his career back) and his current drinking/stimulant use, without confronting him directly — building his own confidence for small, achievable changes first.
  • CBT could target the here-and-now: the thoughts and behaviors tied to his job loss and the drinking that follows it, using the thought → behavior → emotion triangle to interrupt the cycle.
  • Psychodynamic exploration might eventually be useful once he's stabilized — his relationship difficulties and reaction to failure may have roots in earlier relationships and unconscious patterns — but psychodynamic work is slower and less appropriate for an acute crisis.
  • Whatever modality is chosen, the therapeutic alliance matters more than the specific technique — he has to trust the person across from him enough to stay in a very vulnerable position while sober and awake, unlike a surgical patient under anesthesia.

This is a teaching synthesis built from the concepts covered in the lecture — the lecture itself didn't fully work through this case in the asynchronous recording.

Section 03

📜 History: Two Origin Spheres

Psychotherapy grew out of two distinct spheres that still shape the field today: a humanistic sphere (interpersonal, meaning-focused, rooted in religion/spirituality) and a scientific/medical sphere (hypothesis-driven, replicable, testable). Early humanistic therapies weren't well tested; as the scientific method gained ground, therapies were increasingly built to be evaluated for efficacy.

The Humanistic Origins

Mary Baker Eddy (founder of Christian Science) asserted as far back as 1875 that illness could be healed by prayer alone, and that illness was a "mental error" rather than a true physical disorder — an early, extreme version of the idea that mental states can produce physical manifestations. Later editions of her writing even claimed x-ray-confirmed fracture healing through talk therapy alone (almost certainly reflecting normal bone healing, not the treatment).

Phineas Quimby, active in the early-to-mid 19th century and a teacher/influence on Eddy, is credited with an early version of the mind-body concept: that our mental states "carry forward" into physical manifestations in daily life — a primitive ancestor of today's understanding of stress physiology and epigenetics (e.g., stress-related DNA methylation). Quimby was described at the time as a mesmerist and healer — language that placed him outside the medical establishment as medicine professionalized.

🕯️
Early humanistic approaches leaned on connection and belief rather than replicable method — which is exactly why the scientific camp began to pull away: results varied person to person, and not everyone believed the treatment would work in the first place.

The Scientific Turn: Freud

Around 1886, Sigmund Freud — trained as an Austrian neurologist — opened a private practice to study psychopathology, building on hypnosis research he'd seen from Charcot. In 1906, Freud's ideas were introduced to the United States via a lecture at Clark University. Freud's real contribution wasn't necessarily originality — he was one of the first to package these ideas into a digestible, "scientific-style" written form, turning hysteria into a testable theory: a cause (often trauma), a mechanism, and a targeted treatment.

Freud's Famous Cases

Anna O.

Cough, paralysis, sensory loss, hallucinations, loss of consciousness

Treated in collaboration with Josef Breuer; considered the founding case of psychoanalysis and the origin of the phrase "talking cure."

Dora

Aphonia (loss of voice) with no medical explanation

Dream analysis pointed Freud toward an unconscious desire tied to a father figure — the Oedipus complex — and produced what are considered Freud's earliest writings on transference.

Little Hans ⭐ HY

Phobia of horses

Freud interpreted the phobia as displaced fear of castration by an overbearing father, competing for the mother's attention — a textbook Oedipus complex illustration and a frequently tested case.

Wolf Man & Rat Man

Dream analysis; obsessions/compulsions

Wolf Man's dream analysis centered on fear of animals and castration themes. Rat Man presented with obsessions about his father and wife's well-being tied to a disturbing story about rats — considered the first reported "cure" by psychoanalysis. Both cases illustrate how much of early Freudian theory centered on sexual and aggressive drives.

A Parallel Track: The Emmanuel Movement

Around the same era, the Emmanuel Movement paired the Emmanuel Church with medical providers to treat patients with tuberculosis housed in isolation-focused TB hospitals — addressing the toll of being cut off from family and community while severely ill. This produced some of the earliest organized individual and group therapy, delivered mostly by church members rather than physicians — a sharp contrast to the Freudian, physician-led model. It became the basis for the Boston School of Psychopathology.

🗣️
Physician John K. Mitchell, arguing for medicine's claim over the field: "Most earnestly should we insist that the treatment of a patient, whether it be surgical, medical, or psychic, should be... in the hands of a doctor." This is the line in the sand where the medical model began pulling therapy away from clergy and lay healers.

As the medical model took hold, therapy was increasingly expected to be replicable and evidence-backed. Meanwhile, a separate biologic/experimental track was developing in parallel — animal-learning research that would become behaviorism.

Section 04

🐕 Behaviorism

Behaviorists wanted only objective, observable data — no theorizing about unconscious drives. Learning theory research (largely on animals) became the next big shift in psychotherapy, and much of it is ⭐ HY for exams because it's crisp and easy to write test questions about.

Classical Conditioning ⭐ HY

🔔
Definition: pairing a natural, innate response (physiologic — e.g., salivation, fear) with a neutral stimulus that has no inherent connection to it, until the neutral stimulus alone triggers the response.
  • Pavlov's dog — food (innate salivary response) repeatedly paired with a bell (neutral) → eventually the bell alone triggers salivation.
  • Little Albert (Watson) — a loud noise (innate fear response) paired with exposure to a rat (neutral) → the child becomes fearful of the rat itself, demonstrating classical conditioning in humans. Watson championed this objective, "materialistic" data over introspective/"mentalistic" theorizing.
Practice Question
Which of the following is NOT an example of classical conditioning?
A. A dog is shown food and a bell is rung; he salivates each time the bell rings.
B. A rat in a cage is given a piece of food each time it touches a desired button.
C. A loud noise is made each time a child touches a ball; the child becomes scared of balls.
D. A person eats a large sushi meal, coincidentally gets a stomach bug and vomits, and sushi is no longer appealing.
Answer: B. Pressing a button to obtain a reward is operant conditioning (behavior → consequence), not classical conditioning (stimulus-stimulus pairing). A, C, and D all pair a neutral stimulus with an innate response.

Systematic Desensitization

Also called habituation — repeated, graded exposure to a feared stimulus decreases the fear response over time (e.g., climbing progressively higher on a ladder for a fear of heights). Modern versions use technology to scaffold exposure: images → VR → the real environment, sometimes with AI helping pace the transitions (e.g., using vitals like heart rate to judge readiness to advance). Most useful for phobias and anxiety disorders.

Aversive Conditioning

The mirror image of systematic desensitization: pair a noxious/unpleasant stimulus with an undesired behavior to extinguish it. Classic example: disulfiram (Antabuse) + alcohol — drinking while on disulfiram produces an unpleasant physical reaction, so alcohol becomes associated with feeling ill.

Operant Conditioning ⭐ HY

Credited to B.F. Skinner: using a reward or punishment to elicit a desired action (classic image: a rat in a cage learning to press a lever for food, or to avoid a shock).

TermDefinitionExample
ReinforcementGiving or taking something away in response to a desired action, to increase its frequencyRat gets food for pressing a lever
Positive reinforcementGiving a reward for the desired behaviorFood for pressing the lever
Negative reinforcementTaking away an aversive stimulus for the desired behaviorLever press stops an electrified floor
PunishmentA response meant to stop an undesired behavior (trigger is the unwanted action, not the wanted one)Shock delivered after an unwanted action
ExtinctionA learned behavior fades once reinforcement stops entirelyRat stops pressing the lever once food stops appearing
ShapingRewarding successive behaviors that get closer and closer to the target behaviorRewarding the rat for getting nearer the lever, then requiring it get closer each time
ModelingLearning a behavior by observing someone (or something) else do itA toddler learns peekaboo just by watching it repeatedly
🧠
Memory Hook — reinforcement vs. punishment: Reinforcement is triggered by the creature doing what you want (encourages it); punishment is triggered by the creature doing what you don't want (discourages it). Positive/negative just describes whether something is added or removed — not whether it "feels good."

Skinner's Operant Conditioning Quadrants ⭐ HY

A classic exam layout for organizing the four reinforcement/punishment terms — whether a stimulus is added or removed crossed with whether the goal is to increase or decrease a behavior:

Increase behaviorDecrease behavior
Add a stimulusPositive reinforcementPositive punishment
Remove a stimulusNegative reinforcementNegative punishment
⚠️
Limitation: Behaviorism gives too little credit to human cognition — executive function and reasoning can "short-circuit" simple conditioning, which is exactly why the cognitive theorists emerged next.
Section 05

💭 Cognitive Theory

The behaviorists ignored a big piece of the picture: humans have a frontal lobe capable of complex reasoning, and don't respond identically to identical stimuli. Cognitive theorists proposed instead that humans respond to their mental representations of a stimulus — learning is cognitively mediated, and cognition itself is a key lever for therapy.

Albert Ellis

Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT)

Aaron Beck

Cognitive Therapy

Also credited: Michael Mahoney and Donald Meichenbaum (cognitive-behavioral modification) — worth recognizing the names, but unlikely to be tested directly ("who invented X" is a low-yield question format here).

🔁
Core idea: "The interpretation results in the behavior." A person's thoughts and perception of reality — not the events themselves — drive how they feel, act, and see the world. Change the thought, and you can change the downstream feeling or behavior.

Automatic Thoughts

🧠
Memory Hook: the brain is a "lazy organ" — it wants maximum efficiency for minimum energy. Automatic thoughts are the fast, pattern-based assumptions this laziness produces: quick, often unexamined conclusions built from repeated past experience, which may or may not actually be true (e.g., assuming people who wear a certain color are unfriendly because a strict teacher once wore that color).
⚠️
Limitation: Cognitive theory doesn't account well for material that's truly subconscious — if you don't have any awareness of where a thought or pattern originated, it's much harder to change through pure cognitive work alone.
Exploration vs. skill-building: Psychoanalytic/psychodynamic work is fundamentally exploratory — there's no fixed roadmap, which is part of why it tends to run longer. Behavioral, cognitive, and CBT-family therapies are much more skills-based, often with an established goal and a defined path to get there — some (like CBT and DBT) are so manualized that nearly every session is scripted.
Section 06

🧩 The Major Modalities

By the mid-20th century there were dozens of therapy "brands." Research eventually showed that what mattered most wasn't necessarily which theory a therapist used, but whether the therapist believed in it and the patient accepted it as something that could help them — plus the strength of the relationship carrying the work (see Efficacy below). Here are the modalities most likely to come up clinically and on exams.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

Thoughts, behaviors, and emotions feed into each other in a loop
ApproachTeaches skills to identify and change unhelpful thoughts and/or behaviors, which then shifts emotion. Any corner of the triangle can be the entry point.
Types / subtypesNumerous adaptations targeting specific symptoms — CBT-P (psychosis), CBT-I (insomnia), CBT for eating disorders, and more.
Worth knowingDepression example: low energy/interest makes it hard to get out of bed → forcing the behavior (get up, shower, walk the dog) can itself shift the thoughts and emotions, even before "feeling better" arrives on its own.

CBT for Anorexia ⭐ HY

A tie-in from the eating disorders lecture
Cognitive focusChallenges the thought that thinness defines the person's whole worth/identity, and works on the cognitive distortions tying self-worth to weight.
Behavioral focusTargets the restriction itself — e.g., gradually reintroducing higher-fat, higher-calorie foods that had been mentally recategorized as "unhealthy," after medical stabilization.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) ⭐ HY

Created by Marsha Linehan, PhD — for borderline personality disorder
StructureA skills-based, manualized treatment built around 4 modules: emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness.
OriginLinehan developed DBT partly from her own lived experience with BPD — she has spoken publicly (including in a well-known New York Times profile) about how the treatment reflects what helped her.
Also used forAdapted well beyond BPD to many other conditions, but the BPD connection is the one to remember for exams.
🧠
Memory Hook: DBT → BPD. If a question mentions dialectical behavior therapy, think borderline personality disorder first.

Where BPD Fits: Personality Disorder Clusters ⭐ HY

Personality disorders are rigid, inflexible patterns of behavior the person usually isn't aware are a problem (egosyntonic), typically present by early adulthood. They fall into three clusters — a useful map for placing BPD (and knowing why DBT is the modality tied to it):

Cluster A — "Weird"

Odd/eccentric · genetic link to schizophrenia

Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal — poor social relationships, no true psychosis.

Cluster B — "Wild"

Dramatic/erratic · genetic link to mood & substance use disorders

Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic — Borderline is the one paired with DBT and with splitting.

Cluster C — "Worried"

Anxious/fearful · genetic link to anxiety disorders

Avoidant, Obsessive-compulsive (personality type), Dependent.

Interpersonal Therapy (IPT)

Focused squarely on relationships
ApproachA structured, time-limited therapy focused on improving current interpersonal relationships and communication skills — less exploratory than psychodynamic work, more here-and-now than CBT's focus on thought content.
Worth knowingDistinct from the humanistic modalities above — IPT is manualized and diagnosis-focused (often depression), not a general relational philosophy.

Motivational Interviewing (MI)

Working within the patient's own value system
ApproachIdentifies the gap between a patient's stated values and their current behavior, works within their resistance rather than confronting it head-on, and builds confidence toward small, achievable steps.
Classic useSubstance use disorders (especially alcohol) — but increasingly used broadly in primary care for chronic disease management (diabetes, heart failure adherence, etc.).

Humanistic (modern)

"How the person interacts in relationships"
Core ideaDysfunctional relationships and environment drive distress; therapy helps the person understand themselves in relation to others and the world.
Key figuresCarl Rogers (person-centered — unconditional positive regard, reflection); Fritz Perls (Gestalt — intense role-play to safely express relational dynamics); Viktor Frankl (existential approaches). This wave grew after World War II, as the field leaned back toward meaning and away from pure science for a time.
LimitationThe approach can be shaped by the very relational/environmental patterns it's trying to correct.

Supportive Therapy

"You're going to feel better"
ApproachListening, encouragement, and stability — filling in a supportive presence that may be missing elsewhere in the patient's life. Sometimes called (a bit dismissively) a "professional friend."
Best fitAcute crises, medical comorbidity, or acute stressors — this is essentially what's delivered on psychiatric consult-liaison services.
LimitationDoesn't always account for the limits of a relationship built mainly on support.

EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization & Reprocessing)

Trauma-focused; closely related to systematic desensitization
ConceptTrauma creates a fight-or-flight response that becomes misattributed to non-threatening reminders of the traumatic event. EMDR uses an external stimulus (classically a light bar moving back and forth) while the patient discusses the traumatic material, pausing before it becomes unmanageable and shifting attention to a neutral stimulus — aiming to decouple the trauma from its physiologic response.
YieldTesting on EMDR has increased somewhat in recent years, though it's still not top-tier yield.
Section 07

🛋️ Psychodynamic / Psychoanalytic — A Closer Look

The original "talk therapy." Foundational idea: past experiences — many now subconscious — have shaped current behavior, and the work is to move that material from unconscious to conscious understanding.

Approach
Help the patient understand how drives, suppressed experiences, past conflicts, and past relationships are shaping their present.
Limitations
Pays limited attention to current/present-day events; usually a long treatment course; cost can limit access.

Three flavors

SchoolKey concepts
FreudianConscious vs. unconscious; the id, ego, and superego
JungianIndividuation; extraversion vs. introversion
Kleinian (Melanie Klein)Child/adolescent analysis; object relations — extended adult-focused theory downward to children
🧩
Object relations, simplified: every meaningful person we encounter across development becomes an internalized "object" — we distill them down to a mannerism, a guiding principle, or a role, and that internalized object goes on to shape our personality.

Transference & Countertransference ⭐ HY

Transference
The patient unconsciously projects feelings from a past relationship onto the treating provider (e.g., a patient reacts to a therapist as though the therapist "is" their critical parent).
Countertransference
The mirror image — the provider projects their own past feelings onto the patient (e.g., a therapist treats a patient warmly because the patient reminds them of a beloved caregiver).

Freud's Structural Model of the Mind

Id

The drives

Unfiltered urges Freud framed as largely sexual or aggressive — the raw push to meet a need right now.

Ego

Primitive control

Introduces enough restraint to function in society — e.g., sitting through a long lecture instead of walking out to get food.

Superego

Fine-tuned control

Adds social/moral nuance on top of the ego — e.g., pausing the lecture recording instead of just leaving, in case something important is said.

Freud's developmental stages (oral, anal, etc.) are also historically important but lower-yield for modern exams — good to recognize, not worth memorizing in depth.

Practice Question
Little Hans was one of Freud's most famous case reports. His case demonstrated which of the following concepts?
A. Dream analysis
B. Transference
C. Oedipus complex
D. Anal fixation
Answer: C. Little Hans's phobia of horses was interpreted by Freud as displaced fear of castration by his father, tied to competition for his mother's attention — the Oedipus complex.

Defense Mechanisms ⭐ HY

Credited largely to Freud but substantially expanded by his daughter, Anna Freud. Defense mechanisms exist to protect the ego from being exposed to something too threatening or vulnerable — some are considered more "mature," others more "primitive," though how useful that mature/immature split really is remains debated. These are easy to write test questions about, so they're worth knowing cold.

🧠
Memory Hook: "Mature adults wear a SASH" — Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor are the four defenses usually classified as "mature." And for splitting: borders split countries — splitting is the cardinal defense of borderline personality disorder.
DefenseDefinitionExample
DenialRefusing to accept an unbearable piece of realityA patient with concerning symptoms insists nothing is wrong and skips the recommended workup
ProjectionAttributing one's own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone elseA person who cheated on a test becomes convinced their classmates are all cheaters
Reaction formationAdopting the opposite attitude to keep an unacceptable emotion out of awarenessSomeone who unconsciously resents a new sibling becomes their most devoted, over-the-top caretaker
Splitting ⭐Categorizing people as all-good or all-bad, with no in-between; a cardinal feature of borderline personality disorder"You're the only doctor here who actually cares — everyone else on this unit is useless"
DisplacementRedirecting an emotion from its true (often threatening) target onto a safer oneSnapping at a spouse after a bad day with a difficult boss
SublimationChanneling an unacceptable impulse into a socially productive outlet (considered a "mature" defense)A person with aggressive impulses becomes a competitive athlete
SuppressionConsciously (deliberately) pushing an uncomfortable thought or feeling out of awareness — the only defense with a conscious componentDeliberately setting aside anxiety about an exam to focus on the lecture in front of you
RationalizationConstructing a more comfortable, logical-sounding explanation for a distressing outcome"I didn't get the promotion because they don't value hard work here anyway"
RegressionReverting to behavior patterns typical of an earlier developmental stage under stressAn older child starts thumb-sucking again after a new sibling arrives
IdentificationUnconsciously patterning one's own behavior after someone more powerful (can be adaptive or maladaptive)A person bullied by a coach becomes an overly harsh coach themselves
IntellectualizationUsing facts and logic to distance oneself from the emotional weight of a situationFocusing on the technical mechanics of a diagnosis instead of its emotional impact
HumorUsing comedy to express or deflect an otherwise uncomfortable feelingA lecturer uncomfortable with a topic inserts jokes throughout the talk
Acting outExpressing an unacceptable emotion through behavior instead of acknowledging the feeling directlyA teenager who feels ignored gets into repeated disciplinary trouble
UndoingTrying to "magically" reverse a past action through a symbolic later behaviorConfessing to and repaying a theft, then going out of one's way to help the person repeatedly afterward
AltruismManaging personal distress by focusing on helping others (a "mature" defense)A person with low self-esteem devotes significant time to volunteering
DissociationMentally separating from distressing real-life events or from one's own thoughts/feelingsHaving no memory of the details surrounding a traumatic event
IdealizationSeeing another person as more competent or powerful than they really areA patient insists their doctor "always knows exactly what to do"
FixationStaying partially stuck at an earlier, more childish stage of development (contrast with regression, which is moving backward from a stage already passed)A college student still sucks her thumb while studying for a stressful exam
Isolation of affectSeparating a distressing fact from the feeling that would normally go with itDescribing a traumatic event in graphic detail with a completely flat, unaffected tone
Passive aggressionExpressing hostility indirectly, through inaction or subtle resistance rather than open confrontationAn employee who resents a manager keeps "forgetting" to complete assigned tasks on time
RepressionInvoluntarily blocking a distressing thought or feeling from conscious awareness entirely (contrast with suppression, which is a deliberate, conscious, temporary version of the same thing)An adult has no memory of attending counseling during a difficult period in childhood

Two commonly confused pairs: repression (unconscious, involuntary) vs. suppression (conscious, deliberate); and fixation (stuck at a stage, never fully progressed) vs. regression (moving backward from a stage already reached).

Section 08

📊 Does It Work? Efficacy & Common Factors

1952
Early research (looking specifically at psychoanalysis) actually found therapy less efficacious than no treatment at all — a surprising, humbling result that fueled the push for more rigorous research.
1950s–80s
Randomized controlled trials become standard for psychotherapy research; treatment increasingly becomes diagnosis-specific (much like not prescribing an antibiotic for a viral illness) — psychoanalysis, CBT, and behavioral treatments were each built with a specific illness in mind.
1977 ⭐ HY
A landmark meta-analysis found an effect size of ~0.8 — meaning a person receiving psychotherapy had a better outcome than roughly 79–80% of people who didn't receive it for the same diagnosed illness.
🔬
Research bias watch: Early studies found CBT and behavioral treatments superior for depression — but once researchers controlled for "allegiance" (a researcher's own preference for the modality they're testing), that superiority mostly disappeared. A good reminder that "which therapy won the trial" sometimes says as much about who ran the trial as about the therapy itself.

Diagnosis-specific evidence, at a glance

DiagnosisWhat the evidence shows
DepressionCBT is the usual go-to on exams; psychoanalytic approaches are also used. If a question doesn't name a specific evidence-based match, CBT is a reasonable default guess given how broadly it's now indicated.
AnxietyLittle difference found between CBT and psychodynamic treatment.
Alcohol use disorderCBT, motivational interviewing, 12-step programs, and social skills training are all efficacious — no single winner.
Personality disorders (esp. BPD)Most personality disorders lack strong evidence-based treatments; BPD is the best-studied. Some research favors transference-focused therapy over DBT specifically for impulsivity, anger, aggressiveness, and irritability — though DBT remains the most widely taught/tested BPD treatment.

The "Common Factors" / Dodo Bird idea

Across theories, research repeatedly fails to show that any single modality is clearly superior overall — a phenomenon sometimes called the "dodo bird verdict" (everybody wins, in Alice in Wonderland). What matters, according to several researchers:

Jerome Frank
An emotionally charged, confiding relationship; a perceived power to heal; a plausible rationale; and a procedure that's actually followed.
Goldfried
A new, corrective experience for the patient, paired with direct feedback.
Castonguay
Insight, a corrective experience, room to express emotion, and a resulting sense of mastery.
🤝
The therapeutic relationship ⭐ HY: the alliance between patient and treater consistently shows up as one of the strongest predictors of outcome — even in pharmacotherapy. In the TDCRP study, psychiatrists with a strong alliance giving placebo got better results than psychiatrists with a weak alliance giving actual medication. Social skills and simple interpersonal connection between provider and patient measurably move outcomes.

Beyond the relationship itself, fit matters: the patient has to believe in and accept the chosen modality (much like a patient who won't take a medication with a side effect they can't tolerate). Selecting a theory really requires two things to both be true — the therapist must understand and believe in it, and the patient must also believe it can help them.

Role of theory

  • Provides a roadmap for the treatment
  • Gives the therapist a lens for formulating the case
  • Therapist and theory need to be compatible
  • Gives the therapist a way to explain the approach to the patient
Extra detail: what even counts as "scientific"?
CampView
PositivistOnly direct observation counts as valid evidence.
RealistIf a theory is believed correct, what it implies (even something unobservable, like the subconscious) can be treated as real.
PhenomenologicalThe person's own perception of events and actions is itself observable and valid data.
ConstructivistMeaning is constructed by the individual; there's no single objective truth to measure against.
Section 09

⚡ Rapid Review

Classical conditioning
Innate response + neutral stimulus → response transfers to the neutral stimulus (Pavlov's dog, Little Albert).
Operant conditioning
Reward/punishment shapes behavior (Skinner). Know reinforcement vs. punishment vs. extinction vs. shaping vs. modeling.
Systematic desensitization
= habituation. Graded exposure decreases fear (phobias/anxiety).
Aversive conditioning
Noxious stimulus paired with an unwanted behavior (disulfiram + alcohol).
Oedipus complex
Little Hans; unconscious rivalry with the same-sex parent for the opposite-sex parent's attention.
Transference / countertransference
Patient projects past feelings onto the provider / provider projects past feelings onto the patient.
Id / Ego / Superego
Raw drives / basic social restraint / fine-tuned moral-social restraint.
Splitting
All-good/all-bad categorization — cardinal feature of borderline personality disorder.
CBT triangle
Thoughts ↔ behaviors ↔ emotions; enter and change at any vertex.
DBT
Marsha Linehan → borderline personality disorder; 4 modules (emotion regulation, mindfulness, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness).
Motivational interviewing
Substance use (esp. alcohol); works within resistance, highlights values-vs-behavior gaps.
EMDR
Trauma-focused; bilateral stimulation decouples trauma response from neutral cues; related to systematic desensitization.
1977 meta-analysis
Effect size 0.8 → therapy patients outperformed ~79–80% of untreated controls.
Therapeutic alliance
Predicts outcome even in medication trials (TDCRP) — often matters more than the specific modality chosen.

⭐ One-Page High-Yield Summary

Introduction to Therapy — condensed for last-minute review. Full explanations and examples are in the sections above.

Conditioning

Classical: innate response + neutral stimulus → response transfers to the neutral stimulus (Pavlov, Little Albert). Usually involuntary.

Operant: reward/punishment shapes a voluntary behavior (Skinner).

Reinforcement↑ behavior (add/remove stimulus)
Punishment↓ behavior (add/remove stimulus)
Extinctionbehavior fades, reinforcement stops
Shapingreward successive approximations
Modelinglearning by observation
Systematic desensitizationgraded exposure ↓ fear (habituation)
Aversive conditioningnoxious stimulus + unwanted behavior (disulfiram+EtOH)

Skinner's Quadrants

↑ behavior↓ behavior
Add stimulusPositive reinforcementPositive punishment
Remove stimulusNegative reinforcementNegative punishment

Trigger test: reinforcer = creature did what you wanted; punishment = creature did what you didn't want.

Freud's Structural Model

Id — raw drives (sexual/aggressive), unfiltered.

Ego — basic reality-testing restraint.

Superego — fine-tuned social/moral restraint.

Transference: patient projects past feelings onto provider.

Countertransference: provider projects past feelings onto patient.

🧠 Mnemonics

  • SASH = mature defenses: Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor
  • "Borders split countries" — Splitting → Borderline PD
  • Repression = unconscious; Suppression = conscious & deliberate
  • Fixation = stuck at a stage; Regression = slide back to one
  • DBT → BPD (Marsha Linehan, 4 modules)
  • Clusters: A = Weird, B = Wild, C = Worried

Ego Defenses — Quick Definitions

  • Denial — refuses painful reality
  • Projection — attributes own impulse to others
  • Reaction formation — opposite attitude masks true feeling
  • Splitting ⭐ — all-good/all-bad; → BPD
  • Displacement — redirects emotion to a safer target
  • Rationalization — logical excuse to avoid self-blame
  • Regression — reverts to an earlier stage under stress
  • Identification — unconsciously mimics someone powerful
  • Intellectualization — facts/logic to avoid emotion
  • Acting out — behavior instead of acknowledging feeling
  • Undoing — symbolic act "reverses" a past deed
  • Dissociation — detachment from self/memory under stress
  • Idealization — sees another as more perfect than real
  • Fixation — stuck at an earlier developmental stage
  • Isolation of affect — fact without its feeling
  • Passive aggression — indirect hostility, no confrontation
  • Repression — unconscious, involuntary blocking
  • Sublimation (mature) — impulse → productive outlet
  • Altruism (mature) — distress managed via helping others
  • Suppression (mature) — conscious, deliberate, temporary
  • Humor (mature) — comedy deflects discomfort

Modality Quick-Map

CBTdepression, anxiety, broad use

Psychodynamicexploratory, long course

Personality Disorder Clusters

A — Weird: Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal (↔ schizophrenia genetics)

B — Wild: Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic (↔ mood/substance use genetics)

C — Worried: Avoidant, OCPD, Dependent (↔ anxiety genetics)

Efficacy Highlights

1977 meta-analysis: effect size 0.8 → therapy beat ~79–80% of untreated controls.

TDCRP: strong alliance + placebo > weak alliance + real medication.

Common factors (Frank/Goldfried/Castonguay): confiding relationship, corrective experience, insight, mastery — matter more than the specific brand of therapy.

Practice Question Recap

Little Hans demonstrates → Oedipus complex (not transference, not dream analysis).

NOT classical conditioning → the rat-pressing-a-button-for-food example (that's operant conditioning).
